content.text: The bells began before dawn. By sunrise, Silvermoon had realized that they weren't ceremonial.

Their clamor crossed the tiled roofs and gilded spires in ragged waves, one tower answering another until the whole city seemed to shudder with bronze voices. Falanaras stood at the eastern windows of House Dawnspear and watched blue-robed messengers run through streets already thick with people. Servants carried water into the courtyard. Neighbors argued at locked carriage doors. Above them, the pale radiance of Ban’dinoriel trembled across the morning sky.

The barrier had always been easier to feel than to see. It lived in the faint pressure behind his eyes, in the wards humming through stone and silverwood, in the assurance that no hostile army could cross the borders of Quel’Thalas unseen. That morning it flickered hard enough to cast violet bands over the city.

Aelrindor Dawnspear entered behind him, fastening the clasp of an old cuirass. The armor had been made for ceremony and maintained out of habit. Its blue enamel and silver edging remained bright, though the leather beneath had stiffened with age. At his hip hung the narrow sword he wore when House Dawnspear attended court.
“The city muster has called every household capable of bearing arms,” Aelrindor said. “You will report to the Court of the Sun.”
Falanaras turned from the window. “And you?”
“I will see the household secured.”

There were six retainers left in the estate, two of them too old for field service and one unable to walk without a cane. His mother’s sister had taken the youngest servants toward the inner districts during the night. Caelir was in Dalaran, beyond any message they could send. Secured was a word his father used when the truth offered no dignity.
“Come with me,” Falanaras said. “They can use every trained blade at the muster.”

Aelrindor’s expression tightened. He had never been warm, but neither had he been cruel. Affection in House Dawnspear passed through tuition paid, boots replaced before winter, and corrections delivered before strangers could witness an error. He laid one gloved hand on Falanaras’s shoulder.
“Your brother is absent. You are here. Go answer the call.”

A concussion rolled across the city. Crystal chimed in every cabinet. In the courtyard, a dragonhawk shrieked and tore free of its handler. The light of Ban’dinoriel flared white, exposing the bones of Aelrindor’s hand through his glove, then dimmed to a bruised haze.

Falanaras felt the Sunwell beneath the shock. Its presence had no single place within him. It was warmth without heat, a current too constant to notice until fear sharpened his senses. The current faltered, recovered, and carried on with a sour vibration threaded through it.
Aelrindor removed his hand. “When kingdoms break, survival may ask more of you than dignity.”
“That sounds very much like permission to run.”
“If the choice is offered, take it.” His father’s mouth moved in the smallest suggestion of a smile. “Most dead men would.”
It was the last kindness Aelrindor ever gave him.

At the Court of the Sun, officers divided citizens by whatever skills panic allowed them to remember. Those with military training were sent south toward the failing defenses. Magi were pulled into warding circles. Healers vanished into temple wagons. Falanaras admitted to three years of fashionable sword instruction and was handed a spear whose ash shaft had already been darkened by another elf’s blood.
“Keep the point toward the Scourge,” the quartermaster told him. “If they speak, keep it there.”

His company contained jewelers, clerks, gardeners, two apprentices from the royal academies, and a vintner who kept asking when the Farstriders would relieve them. A line soldier with a dented shield tried to teach them how to brace in the time it took officers to argue over which gate had fallen.
Then the southern sky opened.

Ban’dinoriel collapsed in sheets of violet fire. The ward-light poured down the horizon and vanished among the trees. For one breath, every elf in the court stood motionless. The impossible had happened too quickly to understand.
From the walls came a cry taken up by thousands: “The Ranger-General!”

Falanaras was carried south with the company until the city opened before them. Beyond the causeway, the greenwoods churned with undead. Bone wagons rolled beneath the trees. Gargoyles circled above the towers. At the center of the advancing host rode a human in black armor, pale hair streaming behind him, a runeblade shedding mist from its edge.

A blue banner remained upright ahead of the retreating ranger lines, its silver device flashing whenever it caught the failing ward-light. Beneath it, a lone figure loosed arrow after arrow into the Scourge ranks. Distance reduced her to blue, silver, and motion, yet every defender knew the stance. Sylvanas Windrunner held the road while her people fled past her.
The black rider reached her. Steel flashed once in the failing ward-light. The banner fell.

The scream that followed passed through stone. It began as one woman’s agony and spread until it seemed to come from every window, every archway, every open mouth around him. Falanaras dropped his spear and clapped both hands over his ears. The sound remained inside his skull.
Something translucent rose above the road, hair and torn robes streaming in air that did not touch the living. It twisted toward the human prince. Chains of dark magic pulled it back.
The line soldier struck Falanaras between the shoulders. “Spear!”
He snatched it from the paving stones as the first ghouls reached them.

The vintner died without raising his weapon. A ghoul struck him in the chest and folded him over backward. The creature came on with its jaw hanging loose, fingers worn to hooked bone. Falanaras braced too high. The spearpoint skidded across a collarbone and buried itself in the dead elf’s throat.
Rot flooded his mouth and nose. The ghoul clawed its way down the shaft. He shoved until his palms tore, felt the point catch against the spine, and kept shoving after the body stopped moving.

When he looked up, half the company was gone. The remainder fled east through streets filled with smoke and the beating wings of gargoyles, searching for a side gate the Scourge had not reached. No officer called them cowards. No officer remained.
He ran with them for three streets before he remembered his father.

The retreat bent east toward the side gates. House Dawnspear lay west, beyond a district already burning. The western approaches had been overrun, and no organized line remained between the estate and the Scourge. Falanaras slowed at the crossing. A woman seized his sleeve and begged him to help lift her son onto a cart. He did. When the cart moved on, he turned away from the refugees and went home.
He told himself the estate might still be secure. His father might be leading the servants toward safety. He might find the courtyard empty and feel foolish for disobeying the retreat.

The western district answered each hope as he reached it. A dragonhawk lay dying beneath a collapsed balcony, its jeweled tack fused into blackened flesh. Frost coated walls untouched by the morning sun. The fountains ran pink. Along the avenue, corpses had been arranged on their knees by some passing necromancer, faces turned toward the city center.
House Dawnspear’s gates stood open.

One leaf had been torn from its hinges. The bronze sunburst above it hung upside down. Falanaras stepped through with the spear lowered and called for his father. His voice carried across the courtyard, entered the house, and returned unanswered.
The first servant lay in the entrance hall. The second had died near the stairs with a kitchen knife still clenched in both hands. Falanaras knew their names. He could not make himself speak them.

Aelrindor sat against the doors of the family solar. His cuirass had been split below the ribs. Blood soaked the formal sash beneath it and spread over the floor in a dark fan. Three ghouls lay within reach of his ceremonial sword. The blade had broken a handspan above the guard.
Falanaras knelt and touched two fingers to his father’s throat. The skin was cool. Aelrindor’s eyes remained open, fixed on the ruined doorway as if the next attacker had merely kept him waiting.

There should have been grief. Instead, Falanaras noticed that his father’s left boot was unlaced. Aelrindor had lectured him for that exact fault when he was ten. The small disorder horrified him more than the wound.
Something scraped in the solar.

A dead retainer lurched through the doors. One side of his face had been eaten away. Falanaras knew him as Beloran, who had taught both Dawnspear sons to ride and had once carried Falanaras home after a fall. The corpse opened its remaining eye and raised a hatchet.
Falanaras backed into the wall. His spear struck a cabinet and tangled in its carved legs. Beloran swung. The hatchet split the panel beside his head, spraying lacquered wood across his cheek.

A shield rim smashed into the corpse’s temple. The second blow broke its neck. A broad-shouldered soldier stepped over the body, drove his sword down through its skull, and wrenched the blade free with both hands.
“Are you bitten?” he demanded.
Falanaras stared at him.
The soldier grabbed his jaw and turned his head toward the light. He had a square face, blood on one eyebrow, and the flat patience of a man accustomed to asking urgent questions of fools. “Bitten.”
“No.”
“Good. I dislike carrying strangers.” He released him. “Theron Brightshield.”
“Falanaras Dawnspear.”
Theron glanced at Aelrindor, then at the family crest above the solar doors. His expression changed without softening. “I’m sorry.”
The words reached Falanaras from a great distance. “I have to bury him.”
“You have to leave.”
“This is my house.”
Theron looked around the broken hall. “Then remember where it is.”
A crash sounded in the courtyard, followed by the wet cries of ghouls. Theron caught Falanaras by the arm and pulled him upright. Falanaras resisted once. Theron struck him across the face.
“You may hate me outside,” he said.
Falanaras left his father sitting guard over a dead house.

Theron took him through service alleys and walled gardens, avoiding the broad avenues where abominations dragged chains between their swollen hands. The city had become a set of brief decisions: which doorway concealed breathing, which shadow moved against the wind, which cries could still be answered.

They found organized resistance near a bridge choked with refugees. A dozen soldiers held the southern approach behind a wall of overturned carts. Their commander wore blue-and-silver spellbreaker plate and carried a crescent glaive in one hand. Scourge magic struck the shield on his other arm in ropes of green fire. The runes around its rim divided the hostile current and shed it into the paving stones without letting the spell take hold. Rynel answered with a short, flat cast of his glaive. The blade crossed the carts, cut the necromancer’s raised arm, and tore power out through the wound. Green fire burst from the caster’s mouth as the loss became injury. The glaive curved back into Rynel’s hand.
“Brightshield,” the captain called. “You are late.”
“I found a nobleman.”
The captain’s gaze moved over Falanaras’s torn court coat, bloody spear, and empty scabbard. “Did you find the useful part?”
“Uncertain.”
“We will test it.” The captain pointed his glaive toward the carts. “Rynel Starweaver. Hold that gap. If anything dead crosses it, inconvenience it.”

Falanaras took his place beside Theron. His hands had stiffened around the spear. Blood from his split palms made the shaft slick, and his father’s body waited behind him with every step he had taken away. He wanted to turn back. He wanted an officer to forbid it so that obedience could bear the blame.

A ranger dropped from the roof above them and landed badly. One knee struck the stones. Her red-gold hair had come loose from its braids, and black blood streaked one cheek. She carried a bow with three arrows remaining.
Rynel caught her before she fell. “Report.”
She stared south. “The Ranger-General is dead.”
No one answered. The scream still lived behind Falanaras’s eyes.
The ranger swallowed. “He raised her. She was with them when the line broke.”

One of the soldiers cursed her for lying. The ranger crossed the space between them and struck him with her bow. “I watched her kill Taliren,” she said. Her voice remained low, which made the words worse. “She begged us to run before he made her do it.”
Rynel took the bow from her hands before she could strike again. “Your name.”
“Lethira Valeflame.”
He passed her a dead soldier’s quiver. “Valeflame, grieve while shooting. We move when the last cart crosses.”

The next assault came under a rain of burning pitch. Ghouls climbed over the barricade. Skeletal archers fired from balconies already occupied by the Scourge. Lethira’s first arrow took an eye socket. Theron held the gap with shield and shoulder, giving Falanaras room to thrust.

He learned to aim beneath the chin. He learned that a spear trapped in ribs had to be twisted before it could be pulled free. He learned that the Scourge pressed forward without anger, and that their silence between blows was harder to bear than any battle cry.

A necromancer appeared at the far end of the bridge. Frost gathered around his raised hands. Rynel advanced alone. He turned his shield into the spell. The runes resisted the freezing command and divided the impact across his armor, though the force still drove him back a step. His glaive left his hand in a hard, flat cast. The blade cut through the necromancer’s forearm and tore power out through the wound. Cold burst inside the caster as the magical loss became injury; his legs locked beneath him. Lethira’s arrow finished him. The glaive curved back into Rynel’s hand.
Falanaras stared one breath too long.
Rynel drove his glaive through a ghoul reaching for him. “Admire it after we live.”

The last refugee cart crossed. Rynel ordered the bridge supports destroyed and led the survivors east before the dust settled. They numbered twenty-three. By the next side gate they were eighteen. No one asked whether the city could still be held.
The eastern inner gate had become a hospital because its walls still stood.

The wounded lay beneath archways and between the feet of statues. Priests moved through them in white and silver vestments darkened by soot. Their prayers competed with the groans, the shouted names of missing children, and the steady impact of the Scourge against the southern doors. Light flared wherever a healer knelt, brief islands of warmth in the smoke.
Rynel’s survivors were directed to the eastern wall while the refugees passed through. Falanaras tried to follow. His fingers would no longer close around the spear.
“Sit,” Theron said.
“I’m able.”
Theron pressed one thumb into his torn palm. Falanaras nearly dropped to his knees.
“Remarkably able,” Lethira said. She had found enough water to wash the black blood from her face. Nothing had removed the vacancy from her eyes.

They pushed him toward the healers. A novice wrapped his hands, apologized for the shortage of salve, and left when someone began choking nearby. Falanaras sat against the wall. Through the gates he could see Silvermoon burning by districts, each blaze reflected in the blue crystal windows of the next.

A child cried out from the center of the hall. Her mother had been pinned beneath a fallen beam, and the soldiers lifting it could not move fast enough. A priestess in torn white robes knelt beside them. Her hair, bright as burnished copper under the gate lamps, had been tied back with a strip cut from her own sleeve.

Falanaras knew High Priestess Liadrin by reputation. House Dawnspear had attended ceremonies where she stood near the Sunstrider dais, distant and immaculate beneath the temple vaults. The woman on the floor had blood to both elbows. One side of her face was blistered. When she called upon the Light, her voice broke on the prayer.

Gold flooded the space beneath the beam. The trapped woman arched with a cry as crushed flesh drew together. Liadrin shook under the effort. She kept one hand over the wound and reached blindly for the child with the other.
“Look at me,” she told the girl. “Keep your eyes here. The Light has not abandoned this place.”
The child clung to her wrist. Liadrin did not pull away, even after the soldiers freed the mother and carried her toward the eastern gate.
An armored messenger forced his way through the wounded. “High Priestess. The king is withdrawing to Quel’Danas. Every healer who can ride is ordered north.”
Liadrin looked toward the sealed doors as another blow shook dust from the arch. Fatigue hollowed her expression. Faith held beneath it, fierce enough to resemble anger.
She placed the child’s hand in a novice’s keeping and rose. “Then find me a hawkstrider.”
As she passed, her gaze caught on Falanaras’s bandaged hands. “Can you still hold a weapon?”
He closed his fingers and lied. “Yes.”
“Good. Hold long enough for someone else to pass you.” She touched two fingers to his brow. Warmth moved through him, slight and immediate. “Then pass yourself.”
The Light vanished when she turned away. Falanaras watched her go through the eastern arch toward the stables, carrying only a bloodstained staff and the certainty that the Light still listened.
He would remember that certainty long after he learned what had become of it.
The southern doors split before Liadrin’s hawkstrider cleared the gate.
Rynel’s voice rose over the first rush of dead. “All wounded who can walk, east through the side gate. Those who cannot, carry them. Valeflame, roofs. Brightshield, with me. Dawnspear—”
Falanaras picked up his spear.
“—try to remain useful.”
They escaped Silvermoon through an eastern side gate while the city died behind them.

Rynel led them along an irrigation road toward a rise overlooking the coast. Refugees moved among the orchards in broken columns. Some carried silver caskets from family shrines. Others carried nothing. Above the trees, Silvermoon’s tallest spires burned from within, blue crystal turning white before it burst.

The Scourge did not stop at the capital. Their main host drove north toward Quel’Danas, trampling gardens, villas, and bodies into one broad road of decay. The island lay beyond the strait beneath a sky crowded with smoke. Elven ships burned near its piers. Among the defenders, one blue banner still flew, its silver phoenix marking the Sunstrider line.
“The king,” someone whispered.

Falanaras had seen Anasterian Sunstrider only during public rites, an ancient figure beneath layers of blue and silver. On the island he was too distant to distinguish from the guard around him. The royal blade announced him instead. Fire leapt high over the Scourge ranks each time Felo’melorn struck, bright enough to be seen across the water.

The refugees on the rise began to cheer. The sound was ragged, almost embarrassed at first. It grew as the fire advanced. Falanaras joined them. For several breaths, the king was the kingdom, and the kingdom still fought.
A line of blue-white frost crossed the island.
Felo’melorn’s flame vanished. The phoenix banner dipped into the mass of dead and did not rise again.
The cheering ended. Lethira lowered her bow. Theron removed his helmet, though no prayer was spoken. Rynel kept watching the island with his glaive braced against the ground.
“Captain,” Theron said quietly. “What do we do?”

Rynel looked over the refugees: children with burned faces, magistrates holding kitchen knives, soldiers who had thrown away shields to carry the wounded. “We prevent the Scourge from reaching this hill.”
It was too small an answer for a fallen king. It was the only answer anyone had.

They built a defense from orchard walls and abandoned wagons. Falanaras stood between Theron and a woman who had lost two fingers. Lethira climbed an apple tree blackened by passing necromancy. Rynel paced the line, correcting grips and moving the most frightened defenders away from the center.
The expected attack never came.

On Quel’Danas, darkness gathered above the Sunwell. It rose in a column shot through with green and violet fire. The pressure within Falanaras deepened. The sacred current that had touched every day of his life drew taut, strained by a force on the other side of the water.
Then something entered it.

Cold poured through Falanaras without touching his skin. He tasted grave soil. His heart lurched into a rhythm that belonged to another body, slowed, and stopped for one impossible beat. Around him, elves cried out and fell. Lethira dropped from the tree. Theron caught the wall with both hands. Even Rynel bent beneath the violation.

The Sunwell remained. Falanaras could still feel it, vast and intimate. Its radiance had been fouled. Necromantic power moved through the old current, carrying whispers in a language that dragged at the dead. The corruption reached into every elf on the hill because the Sunwell had always reached them. There was nowhere inside himself to close a door against it.
On the island, the column burst outward. A figure rose within it, tall and skeletal, robes streaming around a body remade by death. The Scourge answered with a roar that rolled across the strait.

Falanaras vomited beside the wall. When he could breathe again, he found Theron kneeling near him. Blood ran from Theron’s nose. Lethira sat with both arms wrapped around herself, staring toward Quel’Danas.
“What did he do?” she asked.
No one knew enough to answer.

The black-armored prince left the island before nightfall. His army turned south along the road it had carved through Quel’Thalas. From the hill, the survivors watched ranks of undead pass beneath Silvermoon’s ruined towers, carrying their new lich toward another war. Scourge detachments remained in the forests and among the fallen, but the great host did not look back.
The living were left with the kingdom he had finished using.
For three days, survival consisted of counting.

They counted the wounded who needed water, the bodies that had to be burned before necromancers found them, the arrows left in ranger quivers, the streets passable beneath fallen masonry. They counted families at the refugee camps and stopped asking why so few names received answers. Smoke concealed the sun. The corrupted pulse of the Sunwell lingered beneath every task, faint at times, suddenly nauseating at others.

Rynel made soldiers of whoever continued reporting to him. Theron organized water parties. Lethira ranged the eastern woods and returned each evening with fewer arrows and no conversation. Falanaras carried stretchers until his palms bled through Liadrin’s bandages, then wrapped them again and carried more.
On the fourth morning, Rynel found him preparing to enter Silvermoon alone.
“House Dawnspear,” Falanaras said before the captain could ask. “My father is there.”
Rynel studied him. “Dead?”
“Yes.”
“Then he can wait another hour.” Rynel called to Theron for shovels and to Lethira for a route through the western quarter. “No one enters alone.”
They returned as four.

House Dawnspear had burned during their absence. The solar roof had collapsed, but Aelrindor remained where Falanaras had left him. They carried him into the courtyard on a torn door. Theron and Rynel dug beneath an old silverwood whose leaves had shriveled in the Sunwell’s corruption. Lethira searched the surrounding houses for other dead who still had someone to name them.

Falanaras removed the broken ceremonial sword from his father’s hand. He considered taking it. The weapon had never been meant for war, and war had already judged it. He laid it over Aelrindor’s chest instead.
He spoke the Dawnspear funerary blessing. Halfway through, the words escaped him. Theron supplied the next line. His pronunciation was poor. Falanaras finished with him anyway.
When the grave was closed, Rynel waited beside it while Theron and Lethira moved to the gate.
“You were conscripted for the emergency,” the captain said. “The authority that issued the order may no longer exist. You can remain with the refugee camp as a civilian.”

Falanaras looked at the house. Its open windows showed fire-blackened rooms, each stripped of purpose. His father lay beneath the tree. Caelir remained somewhere beyond the ruined kingdom, alive if fortune had spared him. Everything Falanaras possessed could be carried on his body, and most of it had belonged to dead soldiers.
At the gate, Theron pretended not to listen. Lethira made no such effort.
“If I remain,” Falanaras said, “will you train me?”
“Your spear work is terrible.”
“I had noticed.”
“Your discipline is worse. You abandoned a retreat order, nearly died in a private residence, and required Brightshield to retrieve you.”
Falanaras accepted each charge. “Will you train me?”
Rynel’s gaze settled on the fresh grave. “All of that can be trained. The desire to remain cannot.”
He drew himself upright despite the dried blood between the plates of his armor. “Swear that you will serve Quel’Thalas, obey commands, and place the survival of its people before all else”

The old words had belonged to soldiers of an unbroken kingdom. Here they sounded stripped of ceremony. No witnesses stood in polished ranks. No trumpets answered. Smoke moved through the branches above Aelrindor’s grave.

Falanaras thought of the woman who had begged him to lift her son, of Liadrin holding a child’s hand, of Anasterian’s fire dying across the water. He thought of his father telling him to run if the choice came.
The choice had come. It had led him back to the dead. He wanted another.
“I swear.”
Rynel offered his forearm. Falanaras clasped it with both bandaged hands.
“Report at dawn,” the captain said.
“Where?”
Rynel looked beyond the ruined gate toward the smoke over Silvermoon. “Wherever there are still living people.”
They left House Dawnspear together. Falanaras did not look back again. Ahead, the wounded waited for water, the dead waited for fire, and the survivors had begun the work of finding one another.
